erythrae.t: Ionian city on the peninsula facing Chios, home of a famous Sibyl and member of the twelve-city Ionian League.
erythrae.o: Erythrae stood on the coast of the peninsula opposite Chios, founded by tradition by Cnopus, a son of Codrus of Athens, with mixed settlers c. 1000 BCE. It joined the Ionian League and, as an early rival of Chios, fought several wars with the island.
erythrae.r: The Erythraean Sibyl, a prophetess of Apollo, gave the city renown. Erythrae was governed by aristocracies and later oligarchies and democracies, and sent eight ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE. An Athenian decree of the 450s BCE imposed a democratic constitution and garrison on it as a Delian League member.
erythrae.e: Erythrae revolted from Athens in 412 BCE and later swung between Persian, Athenian and Macedonian influence. In the Hellenistic period it was a free city, allied to Rome from the war against Antiochus III, and passed into the province of Asia after 133 BCE.

empire-of-thessalonica.t: Short-lived Greek empire founded when Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus took Thessalonica in 1224 and claimed the Byzantine throne.
empire-of-thessalonica.o: Theodore Komnenos Doukas, ruler of the Despotate of Epirus, steadily conquered the Kingdom of Thessalonica and captured the city in 1224. Around 1227 he was crowned emperor by Demetrios Chomatenos, archbishop of Ohrid, challenging the Empire of Nicaea for leadership of the Byzantine world and preparing to march on Constantinople.
empire-of-thessalonica.r: Theodore ruled a realm stretching from the Adriatic to Thrace, with Byzantine court titles and administration, and quarrelled with Nicaea's patriarch over church authority. In 1230 he attacked Bulgaria but was defeated and captured by Ivan Asen II at Klokotnitsa and later blinded. His brother Manuel then ruled as a Bulgarian client.
empire-of-thessalonica.e: Theodore regained Thessalonica for his son John, who in 1242 had to accept the lesser title of despot from John III Vatatzes. In 1246 Vatatzes took Thessalonica from John's brother Demetrios, annexing it to the Empire of Nicaea.

emirate-of-nejd.t: The second Saudi state, which revived Al Saud rule from Riyadh after the destruction of Diriyah, until the Rashidis overthrew it.
emirate-of-nejd.o: Six years after the Ottoman-Egyptian destruction of the Emirate of Diriyah, Turki ibn Abdullah, a grandson of Muhammad ibn Saud, drove the Egyptian garrison from Riyadh in 1824 and made it his capital. He restored Saudi rule over Najd and al-Hasa and renewed the alliance with the Wahhabi scholars.
emirate-of-nejd.r: The emirate was smaller than its predecessor and avoided war with the Ottoman Empire, leaving the holy cities alone. Faisal ibn Turki, who ruled twice, consolidated it; between his reigns Egypt occupied Riyadh again from 1838 to 1843. The state taxed oasis farmers and tribes and drew on Gulf trade through al-Hasa and Qatif. The Emirate of Jabal Shammar in the north was at first a loyal ally.
emirate-of-nejd.e: After Faisal died in 1865, his sons Abdullah and Saud fought a long civil war, and the Ottomans took al-Hasa in 1871. Muhammad ibn Rashid of Ha'il took Riyadh in 1887 and defeated the Al Saud at Mulayda in 1891; the family fled to the Sheikhdom of Kuwait.

electorate-of-cologne.t: The prince-archbishopric of Cologne, one of the seven electors, whose archbishops crowned German kings and ruled a long strip of the Rhineland.
electorate-of-cologne.o: Cologne had been an archbishopric since the 8th century. In 953 Otto I made his brother Bruno archbishop and also duke of Lotharingia, founding the temporal power of the see. Grants of counties and, in 1180, the Duchy of Westphalia after the fall of Henry the Lion made the archbishops major territorial princes.
electorate-of-cologne.r: The Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed the archbishop as one of the seven electors and arch-chancellor of Italy. After the citizens defeated Archbishop Engelbert II in 1262 and the Battle of Worringen in 1288, Cologne became a free city, and the electors moved to Bonn. The Wittelsbach family held the see from 1583 to 1761, building the palaces at Brühl and Bonn.
electorate-of-cologne.e: French revolutionary armies took the Rhineland in 1794, and the electorate was dissolved in 1803; Westphalia went to Hesse-Darmstadt and other lands to Nassau. After 1815 the territories became Prussian. Cologne Cathedral, begun in 1248, was completed in 1880.

erdini.t: People of north-western Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, usually placed around Lough Erne and linked by name with the Érainn.
erdini.o: The Erdini are named in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, placed inland in the north-west of Ireland, usually located around Lough Erne in modern Fermanagh and neighbouring parts of Donegal. Their name is often compared with Erne and with the Érainn, a population group of early Irish genealogies.
erdini.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The lakeland around Lough Erne was well suited to crannogs and cattle farming, and if the name link with the Érainn holds, they belonged to a widespread group that early Irish historians regarded as one of the ancient peoples of Ireland.
erdini.e: The Erdini do not reappear in any source. Their territory later fell within the lands of the Kingdom of Airgialla and the northern Uí Néill.

estado-novo-portugal.t: Salazar's authoritarian New State, one of Europe's longest-lived dictatorships, which fought to keep Portugal's African empire.
estado-novo-portugal.o: The constitution of 1933, approved by plebiscite, turned the Ditadura Nacional into a corporatist regime under prime minister António de Oliveira Salazar, inspired by Catholic social teaching and the idea of an organic nation.
estado-novo-portugal.r: The regime banned parties except the National Union, censored the press and used the PVDE, later PIDE, secret police and the Tarrafal prison camp against opponents. Portugal stayed neutral in the Second World War, leased the Azores to the Allies and joined NATO in 1949. Its economy remained poor, prompting mass emigration, while from 1961 it fought costly colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.
estado-novo-portugal.e: Marcelo Caetano succeeded Salazar in 1968 but failed to end the wars. On 25 April 1974 the Armed Forces Movement overthrew the regime in the Carnation Revolution, founding the Third Portuguese Republic.

electorate-of-baden.t: Baden's three years as an electorate, when the Napoleonic settlement doubled its territory and set it on the way to a grand duchy.
electorate-of-baden.o: Margrave Charles Frederick had united the two Baden margraviates in 1771. In the Imperial Recess of 1803 he gained the Palatinate's right-bank lands around Heidelberg and Mannheim, parts of the bishoprics of Constance, Basel, Speyer and Strasbourg, and several imperial cities, and was raised to elector.
electorate-of-baden.r: Charles Frederick was a reforming ruler who had abolished serfdom in 1783. As elector he integrated the new lands, whose Catholic and Protestant populations had to be combined, with a new administration and courts, and the University of Heidelberg was reorganised in 1803. Baden allied with Napoleon in the 1805 campaign.
electorate-of-baden.e: After the Peace of Pressburg Baden gained the Breisgau from Austria. In 1806 it joined the Confederation of the Rhine and Charles Frederick took the title of Grand Duke, forming the Grand Duchy of Baden.

early-dynastic-egypt.t: The First and Second Dynasties, which turned a newly united Nile valley into the kingdom of the pharaohs.
early-dynastic-egypt.o: Egypt was united around 3100 BCE when the Thinite king Narmer, followed by Hor-Aha (often identified with the legendary Menes), brought the Delta under the southern kingship. A new capital, Memphis, was founded where the Nile valley meets the Delta, and the First Dynasty began, succeeding the Proto-kingdom of Thinis.
early-dynastic-egypt.r: The kings of the First and Second Dynasties created the lasting institutions of pharaonic Egypt: a court and treasury, taxation recorded in hieroglyphs, the double crown and the royal titulary. Early First Dynasty kings were buried at Abydos with sacrificed retainers, while officials built great mastaba tombs at Saqqara. Den first used the title 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt', and expeditions reached Sinai and Nubia for copper and stone.
early-dynastic-egypt.e: The Second Dynasty saw unrest, with Peribsen adopting Seth rather than Horus as his patron, before Khasekhemwy reunited the country. His successors of the Third Dynasty, from around 2686 BCE, opened the Old Kingdom of Egypt and its age of pyramid building.

eastern-zhou.t: The age of the Zhou kings at Luoyang, whose real power faded while the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods produced Confucius, Laozi and the Hundred Schools of Thought.
eastern-zhou.o: After the Quanrong sacked Haojing in 771 BCE, King Ping moved the court east to Luoyi (Luoyang), under the protection of the State of Jin and the State of Zheng, beginning the Eastern Zhou.
eastern-zhou.r: The kings kept their ritual supremacy but lost real authority. In the Spring and Autumn period (770 to 476 BCE) hegemons such as the State of Qi and the State of Jin led the states in the king's name; in the Warring States period the great states fought wars of annihilation. Iron tools, coinage, cities and bureaucracies spread, and thinkers from Confucius to Han Feizi debated how to restore order.
eastern-zhou.e: The royal domain split into the Duchy of Western Zhou and the Duchy of Eastern Zhou. In 256 BCE the State of Qin seized Wangcheng and King Nan, the last Zhou king, died. Its intellectual legacy shaped Chinese civilisation for the next two thousand years.
eastern-zhou.re: Zhou ancestral religion and worship of Heaven

emirate-of-afghanistan.t: The Barakzai state that reunited Afghanistan, fought two wars with Britain and had its borders fixed by the Great Game.
emirate-of-afghanistan.o: After the collapse of Sadozai power, Dost Mohammad Khan of the Barakzai clan took Kabul in 1826 and assumed the title emir in 1834, building on Barakzai control from 1823. He was deposed by a British invasion in 1839 during the First Anglo-Afghan War but returned in 1842 and reunited Kandahar and Herat.
emirate-of-afghanistan.r: The emirs ruled a fragmented tribal society, with power resting on Pashtun tribal chiefs. After the Second Anglo-Afghan War of 1878 to 1880, Abdur Rahman Khan, the 'Iron Emir', centralised power, crushed revolts and annexed the Hazarajat, while Britain controlled foreign policy. The Durand Line of 1893 and Anglo-Russian agreements set the borders.
emirate-of-afghanistan.e: In 1919 Amanullah Khan fought the Third Anglo-Afghan War and won full independence. In 1926 he took the title king, turning the emirate into the Kingdom of Afghanistan.

eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The last Memphite kings after the collapse of the Old Kingdom, a dynasty of many brief reigns at the start of the First Intermediate Period.
eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: After the long reign of Pepi II and the end of the Sixth Dynasty, a line of kings at Memphis claimed to continue the Old Kingdom of Egypt around 2181 BCE. Manetho's Seventh Dynasty, of 'seventy kings in seventy days', is now usually regarded as fictitious, and its kings are counted with the Eighth.
eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Abydos king list names around a dozen or more rulers in roughly twenty years, most known only by name. Qakare Ibi built a small pyramid at Saqqara inscribed with Pyramid Texts, and decrees of Neferkauhor found at Coptos show royal favour granted to a powerful local family. Real power was passing to provincial governors, and Nile floods appear to have been low.
eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 2160 BCE the Memphite line was displaced by rulers from Herakleopolis, who founded the Herakleopolitan Kingdom. Its brief, obscure history marks the end of Old Kingdom unity and the beginning of the First Intermediate Period.

estado-novo-brazil.t: Getúlio Vargas's authoritarian New State, which built modern Brazil's labour laws and heavy industry and sent troops to fight in Europe.
estado-novo-brazil.o: On 10 November 1937 Getúlio Vargas, president of the Second Brazilian Republic, closed Congress with army support and imposed a new constitution modelled on European authoritarian regimes, creating the Estado Novo, or New State. Elections planned for 1938 were cancelled.
estado-novo-brazil.r: Vargas ruled by decree, abolished political parties and censored the press through the Department of Press and Propaganda. He centralised power, burning state flags in a public ceremony. He introduced a minimum wage in 1940 and the Consolidation of Labour Laws in 1943, winning working-class support. The state founded the National Steel Company at Volta Redonda. Brazil joined the Allies in 1942 and sent an expeditionary force to Italy in 1944.
estado-novo-brazil.e: As the war ended, pressure for democracy grew, and the military deposed Vargas on 29 October 1945. Elections followed, and the constitution of 1946 created the Fourth Brazilian Republic. Vargas returned to power by election in 1951.

elisyces.t: Iberian-influenced people of the coastal plain around Narbonne, among the first inhabitants of Gaul named in Greek writing.
elisyces.o: Known only from a handful of Greek sources. Hecataeus of Miletus names them around 500 BCE, and Herodotus lists Elisyces among the mercenaries hired by Carthage for the Battle of Himera in Sicily in 480 BCE. They held the Languedoc coast between the Pyrenees and the Hérault, with Naro, the oppidum of Montlaurès beside Narbonne, as their main centre.
elisyces.r: Archaeology suggests a mixed culture with strong Iberian features: Iberian script on pottery and lead tablets, fortified hilltop settlements such as Ensérune, and busy exchange with Greek Massalia and Emporion in wine, painted pottery and metals.
elisyces.e: The name fades from the record by the 3rd century BCE, when Celtic Volcae dominated the region. In 118 BCE Rome founded the colony of Narbo Martius next to Montlaurès, which became the capital of Gallia Narbonensis.

eretria.t: Euboean city that helped found Greek colonies in Italy and the north Aegean, and whose support for the Ionian Revolt brought Persian destruction in 490 BCE.
eretria.o: Eretria grew on the south coast of Euboea, facing Attica, in the 8th century BCE, possibly succeeding the earlier settlement at Lefkandi. With Chalcis it was a pioneer of long-distance Greek trade, and their rivalry over the Lelantine plain became the Lelantine War.
eretria.r: Eretrians joined Chalcis in founding Pithekoussai and settled Methone in Macedonia and, by tradition, Corcyra before the Corinthians. It was ruled by aristocracies of horse-breeders. Eretria sent five ships to help Miletus in 499 BCE, sharing in the burning of Sardis. Its later theatre and gymnasium are among the best-preserved on Euboea.
eretria.e: Persia sacked Eretria in 490 BCE and deported its people. Rebuilt, it joined the Delian League and later hosted the philosopher Menedemus. Rome sacked it in 198 BCE, and it lost independence in 146 BCE.
eretria.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Daphnephoros

elis.t: City-state of the north-western Peloponnese that controlled the sanctuary of Olympia and organised the Olympic Games.
elis.o: Elis occupied the fertile lowlands of the Peneios in the north-western Peloponnese, settled by north-west Greek speakers in the early Iron Age. For centuries its people lived in villages; the Eleans won control of the sanctuary of Olympia from Pisa in the 6th century BCE, and the city of Elis was formed by synoecism in 471 BCE.
elis.r: Elis supervised the Olympic Games through officials called Hellanodikai, and its territory was regarded as sacred during the festival. It had an aristocracy and later a democracy, and its land produced horses and flax. Elis produced the sophist Hippias and the sceptic philosopher Pyrrho.
elis.e: Sparta defeated Elis in a war c. 402 to 400 BCE and stripped it of Triphylia. In the Hellenistic period Elis allied with the Aetolian League before joining the Achaean League in 191 BCE, and passed under Rome in 146 BCE.
elis.re: Greek religion; cult of Olympian Zeus

estonian-soviet-socialist-republic.t: Soviet Estonia, imposed by annexation in 1940 and ended by the Singing Revolution and the restoration of independence in 1991.
estonian-soviet-socialist-republic.o: The Soviet Union occupied the Republic of Estonia in June 1940 under the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. After rigged elections, a puppet parliament asked to join the Soviet Union, and Estonia was annexed in August 1940. German occupation followed in 1941-1944, and Soviet rule returned in 1944.
estonian-soviet-socialist-republic.r: Soviet rule brought nationalisation, collectivisation and mass deportations, especially in June 1941 and March 1949, when over 20,000 people were sent to Siberia. Large-scale Russian-speaking immigration changed the population, and oil shale industry developed in the north-east. Johannes Käbin led the Communist Party from 1950 to 1978. Estonia's access to Finnish television made it unusually open to Western influence.
estonian-soviet-socialist-republic.e: In the late 1980s the Singing Revolution mobilised mass protest. The Supreme Soviet declared Estonian sovereignty in 1988, and during the failed Moscow coup Estonia declared full independence on 20 August 1991, restoring the Republic of Estonia.

emirate-of-tbilisi.t: A Muslim emirate centred on Tbilisi that ruled the heart of eastern Georgia for nearly four centuries until David the Builder took the city in 1122.
emirate-of-tbilisi.o: Arab armies first took Tbilisi in the 640s, and around 736 the Umayyad general Marwan ibn Muhammad made it the seat of an emir governing Georgian lands. Under the Abbasid Caliphate the emirs turned the strategic city on the Mtkvari into a largely self-governing state.
emirate-of-tbilisi.r: Tbilisi was a prosperous trading city of Muslims, Christians and Jews, with a mint, baths and markets. The emirs, notably the Jaffarid family, often defied Baghdad: Ishaq ibn Ismail's rebellion ended in 853 when the Abbasid general Bugha the Elder burned the city. Later the emir shared power with a council of leading citizens.
emirate-of-tbilisi.e: Weakened by Georgian pressure, the emirate fell under Seljuk control in the 1080s. In 1122 David IV of the Kingdom of Georgia captured Tbilisi after the Battle of Didgori and made it his capital.

ezeritai.t: Slavic tribe of the lower Eurotas valley in Laconia, a tribute-paying neighbour of the Melingoi under Byzantine rule.
ezeritai.o: The Ezeritai, whose name probably comes from the Slavic word for lake, settled in the marshy plain of Helos in southern Laconia during the Slavic migrations into the Peloponnese of the late 6th and 7th centuries. They first appear clearly in Byzantine sources of the 9th and 10th centuries.
ezeritai.r: Like the Melingoi, the Ezeritai kept their own leaders and paid a fixed tribute instead of regular taxes, set by Constantine VII at 300 gold coins a year. They were subdued by Theoktistos Bryennios in the 840s and rebelled again in the 920s under Romanos I, after which their tribute was raised. Little else is recorded of their society.
ezeritai.e: They remained distinct under Frankish rule in the 13th century and are mentioned in the Chronicle of the Morea. Over time they converted to Orthodox Christianity and merged into the Greek population of Laconia, leaving place names as their main trace.
ezeritai.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

emirate-of-asir.t: A highland emirate of south-western Arabia that resisted Egyptian and Ottoman armies for half a century from its base at Abha.
emirate-of-asir.o: Asir, the mountainous region between the Hejaz and Yemen, had joined the Emirate of Diriyah and fought hard against the Egyptian armies of Muhammad Ali. After Diriyah fell in 1818, local leaders took charge, and from 1823 a series of emirs, from 1834 of the Al Aidh family, ruled the region from Abha.
emirate-of-asir.r: The emirs led a confederation of highland tribes, combining Wahhabi-influenced religious leadership with tribal warfare. They fought off Egyptian expeditions in the 1820s and 1830s and raided the Tihama coast and the Yemeni ports. Under A'id ibn Mar'i and his son Muhammad the emirate remained largely independent of the Ottoman Empire despite repeated campaigns.
emirate-of-asir.e: In 1871-1872 an Ottoman army took Abha, and Muhammad ibn A'id was killed. Asir was incorporated into the Yemen Vilayet as a sanjak, and later passed to the Idrisid Emirate of Asir and then to Saudi Arabia.

estonian-self-administration.t: Estonian collaborationist administration under German occupation in 1941-1944, headed by Hjalmar Mäe within Reichskommissariat Ostland.
estonian-self-administration.o: German forces drove the Red Army out of Estonia in summer 1941. The occupiers placed Estonia in the Generalkommissariat Estland within Reichskommissariat Ostland, and in 1941 appointed a Directorate of Estonians led by Hjalmar Mäe to handle local administration.
estonian-self-administration.r: The Self-Administration had limited powers under German control and could not restore independence. It ran local government, schools and the economy, and took part in German policies. Almost all of Estonia's Jews who had not fled were murdered in 1941, and camps such as Klooga held Jews deported from elsewhere. From 1943 Estonian men were conscripted into German units.
estonian-self-administration.e: As the Red Army advanced in September 1944 and the Germans withdrew, Mäe left, and Otto Tief briefly formed a national government in Tallinn on 18 September. Soviet forces took Tallinn on 22 September 1944, restoring the Estonian Soviet Socialist Republic.

emirate-of-bari.t: Short-lived Muslim emirate in Apulia, centred on the port of Bari, which raided southern Italy until Louis II took it in 871.
emirate-of-bari.o: Arab and Berber soldiers, some of them mercenaries hired by the warring Lombard princes, seized Bari around 847 under a leader named Kalfun. From this base on the Adriatic coast they extended control over much of Apulia.
emirate-of-bari.r: Under Mufarraj ibn Sallam and then Sawdan, the last emir, Bari sought recognition from the Abbasid caliph and became an emirate with a congregational mosque. It lived largely from raiding and the slave trade, attacking Lombard and Byzantine territory and monasteries, though Sawdan also dealt diplomatically with Christian neighbours, and a Jewish chronicle recalls him as a figure of learning.
emirate-of-bari.e: The Carolingian emperor Louis II besieged Bari for several years with Lombard allies and Byzantine naval help, taking the city in 871 and capturing Sawdan. The Byzantines occupied Bari in 876, and it became the capital of the Theme of Longobardia.

essequibo.t: The oldest Dutch colony on the Guiana coast, founded as a trading post on the Essequibo river and later a plantation colony that became part of Guyana.
essequibo.o: Dutch traders from Zeeland established a post on the Essequibo river around 1616, at the fort of Kyk-over-al on an island near the meeting of the Essequibo, Mazaruni and Cuyuni rivers. From 1621 the colony was run by the Zeeland chamber of the Dutch West India Company.
essequibo.r: Early Essequibo traded with indigenous peoples for dyes and hardwoods, but sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans gradually took over. The seat of government moved to Fort Zeelandia on Fort Island in the 18th century. Commander Laurens Storm van 's Gravesande, from 1743, opened the neighbouring Demerara river to settlement, which soon outgrew Essequibo, and many British planters settled there. Relations with indigenous peoples relied on gifts and alliances.
essequibo.e: The colony changed hands several times during wars, and Britain occupied it from 1796. It was united with Demerara in 1812 as Demerara-Essequibo, formally ceded to Britain in 1814, and merged into British Guiana in 1831. Venezuela still claims the region west of the Essequibo.

eburones.t: Belgic people between the Meuse and the Rhine who destroyed a Roman legion in 54 BCE and were wiped out by Caesar in revenge.
eburones.o: The Eburones lived between the Meuse and the Rhine, in modern eastern Belgium and the southern Netherlands. Caesar counts them among the Germani Cisrhenani and says they had paid tribute to the Aduatuci.
eburones.r: They were ruled jointly by two kings, Ambiorix and the elderly Catuvolcus. Their stronghold was Atuatuca, where Caesar stationed troops for the winter of 54 BCE.
eburones.e: In 54 BCE Ambiorix lured the legion and a half under Sabinus and Cotta out of Atuatuca and destroyed it. In 53 BCE Caesar invited neighbouring peoples to plunder their land; Catuvolcus poisoned himself with yew, while Ambiorix escaped. Their territory was later settled by the Tungri.

electorate-of-trier.t: The ecclesiastical principality of the archbishops of Trier, one of the seven electors of the Holy Roman Empire, stretching along the Moselle and Rhine.
electorate-of-trier.o: Trier had been an imperial capital in late Roman times and a bishopric since the 3rd century. In 898 King Zwentibold granted Archbishop Ratbod immunity and comital rights over the city, the basis of the archbishops' temporal power. Over the following centuries they built a territory along the Moselle from Trier to Koblenz.
electorate-of-trier.r: Archbishop Baldwin of Luxembourg, brother of Emperor Henry VII, consolidated the territory between 1307 and 1354. The Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed the archbishop as an elector and arch-chancellor for Gaul and Burgundy. The electors moved their residence to Koblenz and Ehrenbreitstein, and Trier kept the Holy Robe relic, exhibited to pilgrims.
electorate-of-trier.e: French revolutionary armies occupied the left bank of the Rhine in 1794. The last elector, Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, fled, and in 1803 the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss dissolved the electorate, its remaining eastern lands going to Nassau-Weilburg. After 1815 most of it became Prussian.

emirate-of-cordoba.t: The independent Umayyad state in al-Andalus founded by a refugee prince in 756, which built the Great Mosque of Córdoba.
emirate-of-cordoba.o: After the Abbasids massacred the Umayyad family in 750, the prince Abd al-Rahman escaped to North Africa and crossed to al-Andalus in 755. Backed by Umayyad clients and Syrian troops, he defeated the governor Yusuf al-Fihri in 756 and became emir at Córdoba, independent of Baghdad.
emirate-of-cordoba.r: The emirs built a centralised state with a professional army, a bureaucracy and a coinage. Abd al-Rahman I began the Great Mosque in 785. Al-Hakam I crushed the revolt of the suburb of Córdoba in 818, and Abd al-Rahman II, patron of the musician Ziryab, brought eastern fashions and repelled the Vikings from Seville in 844. Christians were steadily Arabised and converted.
emirate-of-cordoba.e: From the 880s revolts by muwallads such as Umar ibn Hafsun and local lords split the emirate. Abd al-Rahman III restored control from 912 and in 929 declared himself caliph, turning the emirate into the Caliphate of Córdoba.

eastern-rumelia.t: Autonomous Ottoman province south of the Balkan mountains, created at Berlin to divide Bulgaria and absorbed into it by a bloodless coup in 1885.
eastern-rumelia.o: The Treaty of San Stefano in 1878 had created a large Bulgaria, but the Congress of Berlin split it, leaving the southern part as Eastern Rumelia, an autonomous province of the Ottoman Empire. Its constitution, the Organic Statute, was drafted by an international commission, and Plovdiv became its capital.
eastern-rumelia.r: A Christian governor-general appointed by the sultan with the approval of the Great Powers headed the administration, first Aleko Bogoridi and then Gavril Krastevich, with an elected assembly. The majority population was Bulgarian, with Turkish, Greek and Pomak minorities. Bulgarian became the dominant language of government and schools, and the province's militia was largely Bulgarian.
eastern-rumelia.e: On 6 September 1885 Bulgarian activists and militia in Plovdiv deposed the governor and proclaimed union with the Principality of Bulgaria. Bulgaria then defeated Serbia, and in 1886 the sultan recognised the Bulgarian prince as governor-general, ending the province in practice.

emesene-dynasty.t: Emesa, an Arab priestly kingdom in central Syria whose descendants included the Roman empress Julia Domna and emperor Elagabalus.
emesene-dynasty.o: Sampsigeramus I, an Arab chief, controlled the Orontes valley around Emesa, modern Homs, as the Seleucid Empire collapsed. Pompey recognised him as a client ruler in 64 BCE, founding a dynasty that would last over a century.
emesene-dynasty.r: Its rulers were priests of the sun god Elagabal, worshipped as a black stone at Emesa. They served Rome with archers and soldiers and grew wealthy on the caravan trade of the Syrian desert. Iamblichus I was executed by Mark Antony, but the dynasty soon regained power under Augustus.
emesene-dynasty.e: After Gaius Julius Sohaemus, the kingdom was absorbed into Roman Syria around 72 CE. The priestly family survived, and Julia Domna married Septimius Severus; her great-nephew Elagabalus became emperor in 218 CE.

emirate-of-dhala.t: The Amiri emirate on the highland frontier north of Aden, where the armed revolt against British rule in South Arabia began.
emirate-of-dhala.o: The Amiri family ruled the district of Dhala, a high plateau on the route between Aden and the Yemeni highlands. They became independent of the Qasimid State in the 18th century. The Zaydi imams and later the Ottoman Empire continued to claim the area.
emirate-of-dhala.r: The emir governed through tribal sheikhs and taxed the trade crossing the frontier. Britain brought Dhala into the Aden Protectorate, and the Anglo-Ottoman boundary of 1904 left it on the British side. British political officers and troops were stationed there, and the emirate was a founding member of the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South in 1959.
emirate-of-dhala.e: In 1963 tribesmen of the nearby Radfan mountains launched the armed struggle of the National Liberation Front against the federation. When the NLF took over in 1967 the emirate was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.

ebusus.t: The Punic city of Ibiza, a Carthaginian stronghold whose vast necropolis and Tanit cult make it a key site for Phoenician civilisation in the West.
ebusus.o: Phoenicians had a small trading post at Sa Caleta on Ibiza in the 7th century BCE. According to Diodorus, the city of Ebusus was founded in 654 BCE on the bay of modern Ibiza town, and it soon came under the influence of Carthage.
ebusus.r: Ebusus became one of the most important Punic cities in the western Mediterranean, producing wine, oil, salt, purple dye and pottery, and minting coins showing the god Bes. The Puig des Molins necropolis contains thousands of tombs, and the cave sanctuary of Es Culleram was dedicated to Tanit. It controlled trade with the Balearic Islanders and recruited their slingers.
ebusus.e: Ebusus stayed loyal to Carthage through the Second Punic War, but afterwards made a treaty with Rome. After the Roman conquest of the Balearics in 123 BCE it was increasingly integrated, becoming a Roman municipium under Vespasian while keeping Punic culture for centuries.

euzkadi-1936-1937.t: The first Basque autonomous government, formed during the Spanish Civil War and defeated within a year, after the bombing of Guernica.
euzkadi-1936-1937.o: After the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War, the Second Spanish Republic granted the Basque Country a Statute of Autonomy in October 1936. José Antonio Aguirre of the Basque Nationalist Party was sworn in as first lehendakari under the oak of Guernica on 7 October 1936.
euzkadi-1936-1937.r: The government controlled only Biscay and part of Gipuzkoa. It raised its own army, issued money and passports, and protected the Catholic Church, unlike much of Republican Spain. Bilbao's industry and port were its base, defended by the fortified Iron Ring.
euzkadi-1936-1937.e: Franco's Army of the North attacked in 1937. German and Italian aircraft destroyed Guernica on 26 April 1937, and Bilbao fell on 19 June. Basque troops surrendered to the Italians at Santoña in August. The government went into exile, and Basque autonomy was restored only in 1979.

earldom-of-more.t: Coastal earldom of western Norway whose first great earl, Rognvald Eysteinsson, backed Harald Fairhair and founded the line of the earls of Orkney.
earldom-of-more.o: Møre, the coastal land between Romsdal and the fjords to the south, was a petty kingdom in the 8th century. The sagas say that Harald Fairhair, after conquering it, gave the region to his ally Rognvald Eysteinsson as earl in the late 9th century, joining North and South Møre under one lord.
earldom-of-more.r: The earls held power through their fleets, their great farms and their command of the sea lanes along the coast. Rognvald's family spread overseas: his brother Sigurd became the first Earl of Orkney, his son Torf-Einarr later ruled there, and Norman tradition claimed that Rollo, founder of Normandy, was another son. The earls answered to the king but acted largely on their own.
earldom-of-more.e: Rognvald was killed, according to the sagas, when sons of Harald Fairhair burned him in his hall. His descendants kept the earldom for a time, but by around 1000 Møre was governed directly by the kings of Norway or by the earls of Lade, and it became part of the Kingdom of Norway.

east-francia.t: The eastern Carolingian kingdom created at Verdun in 843, from which the Kingdom of Germany and the Holy Roman Empire developed.
east-francia.o: The Treaty of Verdun in 843 divided the Carolingian empire among the three sons of Louis the Pious. Louis the German received the lands east of the Rhine, together with Mainz, Worms and Speyer on its west bank. He ruled them from palaces such as Regensburg and Frankfurt, and in 870 the Treaty of Meerssen added much of Lotharingia.
east-francia.r: East Francia combined Franks, Saxons, Bavarians, Swabians and Thuringians, each with strong regional identities that grew into stem duchies. Kings moved between palaces and relied on bishops and great abbeys. Arnulf of Carinthia defeated the Vikings on the Dyle in 891 and was crowned emperor in 896, but Magyar raids devastated the kingdom after 900.
east-francia.e: When the last Carolingian, Louis the Child, died in 911, the nobles elected Conrad I of Franconia, then in 919 Henry the Fowler of Saxony. Henry's son Otto I defeated the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955 and was crowned emperor in 962, a date usually taken as the start of the Kingdom of Germany within the Holy Roman Empire.
east-francia.la: Old High German, Old Saxon, Latin

enchelei.t: Illyrian people around Lake Ohrid, linked by Greek legend to the hero Cadmus, among the earliest Illyrian groups named in Greek sources.
enchelei.o: Greek writers from Hecataeus and Herodotus onward place the Enchelei, the 'eel people', near Lake Ohrid and the Drin valley. Myth said Cadmus and Harmonia came to rule them after leaving Thebes, and that their descendants ruled the Illyrians. Little beyond these mentions survives, and their origins are otherwise unknown.
enchelei.r: Known only from scattered Greek references, the Enchelei appear as a tribal people of the lake district around Lychnidus (Ohrid), whose fisheries probably gave them their name. Later authors seem to treat the Sesarethii as the same or a successor people.
enchelei.e: By the 4th century BCE their name fades, and the region around Lake Ohrid appears under the Dassaretae and within the sphere of Macedon and the Illyrian Kingdom.

eastern-province.t: The self-governing Banda Oriental of José Artigas, which pioneered federalism and land reform before being overrun by Portugal.
eastern-province.o: The Banda Oriental, east of the Uruguay river, rose against Spanish Montevideo in 1811 under José Gervasio Artigas. In 1813 a congress of the Eastern Province adopted the Instructions of the Year XIII, demanding independence and a federal union with the other provinces of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata.
eastern-province.r: Buenos Aires rejected the Instructions and captured Montevideo from Spain in 1814. Artigas broke with Buenos Aires and took Montevideo in 1815, governing through a cabildo while leading the wider Federal League. His Provisional Regulation of 1815 distributed confiscated land to poor settlers, indigenous people and freedmen, one of the first agrarian reforms in the Americas.
eastern-province.e: Portuguese troops from Brazil invaded in 1816 and occupied Montevideo in January 1817. The province was annexed as Cisplatina, while Artigas fought on until 1820. Artigas is honoured as the founder of Uruguayan nationhood.

ephesus.t: Ionian port city of the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders, and later the capital of Roman Asia.
ephesus.o: Ionian settlers led, by tradition, by Androclus, son of Codrus of Athens, founded Ephesus near the mouth of the Cayster c. 1000 BCE, beside a native cult of a mother goddess. The Greeks identified her with Artemis, and her sanctuary became the city's focus. Ephesus was one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League.
ephesus.r: Ephesus prospered from trade between the Aegean and inner Anatolia. Croesus of the Kingdom of Lydia took the city c. 560 BCE, ousting the tyrant Pindarus, and paid for columns of the great marble Artemision. The philosopher Heraclitus lived there. Under the Achaemenid Empire and then the Delian League it kept its temple economy, with the sanctuary acting as a bank and place of asylum.
ephesus.e: The temple burned in 356 BCE and was rebuilt in grander form. Lysimachus moved the city to a new site c. 290 BCE. After Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Pergamene rule, Ephesus passed to Rome in 133 BCE and became the chief city of the province of Asia.
ephesus.re: Greek religion; cult of Artemis of Ephesus

emirate-of-beihan.t: A frontier emirate in Wadi Bayhan, ancient heart of Qataban, whose sharifs were staunch British allies against Yemen.
emirate-of-beihan.o: Wadi Bayhan, once the core of the Kingdom of Qataban, was by the 19th century divided between local tribes and a family of sharifs, descendants of the Prophet, who emerged as emirs around 1800 with their seat at Suq Abdullah.
emirate-of-beihan.r: Beihan lay on the disputed border between the Aden Protectorate and the imams' Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen, and clashes there were frequent in the 1950s. Its ruling sharif, Husayn ibn Ahmad al-Habili, was one of Britain's firmest allies and a founding figure of the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South in 1959. Agriculture depended on seasonal floods.
emirate-of-beihan.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over the region and the emirate was incorporated into South Yemen; its ruling family went into exile.

earldom-of-ormond.t: The great Butler lordship of Kilkenny and Tipperary, for four centuries one of Ireland's most powerful Anglo-Irish dynasties and a loyal crown ally.
earldom-of-ormond.o: The Butlers descended from Theobald Walter, who came to Ireland with Prince John in 1185 and held the hereditary office of butler of Ireland. In 1328 James Butler became the first Earl of Ormond and was granted palatine rights over Tipperary.
earldom-of-ormond.r: The earls ruled their palatinate from Kilkenny Castle, bought in 1391, and Carrick-on-Suir, with their own courts. Generally loyal to the crown, they were rivals of the Kildare and Desmond FitzGeralds. Thomas Butler, the 10th Earl, helped crush the Desmond rebellions; James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormonde, was Lord Lieutenant under Charles II.
earldom-of-ormond.e: James Butler, 2nd Duke, joined the Jacobites and was attainted in 1715, and the Tipperary palatinate was abolished in 1716. The Butlers kept Kilkenny Castle until 1967.

electorate-of-mainz.t: The most powerful church state of the Holy Roman Empire, whose archbishop was arch-chancellor of Germany and convened the elections of kings.
electorate-of-mainz.o: The see of Mainz was raised to an archbishopric around 780 to 782, building on the work of Saint Boniface, archbishop there from 746. Its province became the largest in Latin Christendom. Royal grants from the Ottonians onwards gave the archbishops temporal lordship over Mainz and scattered lands along the Main, the Rhine, in Hesse and the Eichsfeld.
electorate-of-mainz.r: From 965 the archbishop held the title of arch-chancellor of Germany, and the Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed him as first among the seven prince-electors, presiding over imperial elections. Mainz was governed by its cathedral chapter and archbishop. Gutenberg invented printing there in the 1450s, and the university was founded in 1477.
electorate-of-mainz.e: France occupied the left bank of the Rhine during the Revolutionary Wars, and the short-lived Republic of Mainz was proclaimed in 1793. The Reichsdeputationshauptschluss of 1803 dissolved the electorate; its last elector, Karl Theodor von Dalberg, kept a state centred on Aschaffenburg and Regensburg.

emar.t: Emar, a Syrian trading city at the great bend of the Euphrates whose Late Bronze Age tablets show daily life and ritual under Hittite overlordship.
emar.o: Emar is named in the archives of Ebla and Mari as a market town where caravans from Syria met boats on the Euphrates. Its position at the river's westward bend made it a key stage on the route between Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean from the mid-3rd millennium BCE.
emar.r: In the 14th century BCE the city was rebuilt on a new site as the capital of the land of Ashtata, governed by local kings and a council of elders under the Viceroyalty of Carchemish and the Hittite Empire. Over a thousand Akkadian tablets record land sales, adoptions, wills and the festivals of the god Dagan.
emar.e: Emar was destroyed c. 1185 BCE in the wave of violence that ended the Late Bronze Age. Its site at Meskene was partly flooded by Lake Assad after the Tabqa Dam, and French salvage excavations in the 1970s recovered its archives.

early-duchy-of-aquitaine.t: Independent duchy of south-western Gaul whose dukes defied the Franks and fought the Umayyad advance in the 8th century.
early-duchy-of-aquitaine.o: As Merovingian power weakened in the mid 7th century, the region south of the Loire came under semi-independent dukes. Felix, a nobleman of Toulouse, is recorded around 660, followed by Lupus and then Odo, called the Great, who ruled Aquitaine and Gascony from around 700.
early-duchy-of-aquitaine.r: The duchy kept a strong Gallo-Roman identity and Roman law. Odo defeated an Umayyad army besieging Toulouse in 721, one of the first checks on the Muslim advance, but was routed near Bordeaux in 732 and had to seek help from Charles Martel, joining him at the battle near Tours.
early-duchy-of-aquitaine.e: Odo's son Hunald and grandson Waiofar resisted the Carolingians, but Pippin the Short waged yearly wars against Waiofar until his murder in 768. A last rising under a second Hunald was crushed by Charlemagne in 769, and Aquitaine became part of the Kingdom of the Franks.

emirate-of-bohtan.t: A Kurdish emirate at Cizre on the Tigris, setting of the epic Mem u Zin and seat of Bedir Khan, whose revolt shaped modern Kurdish nationalism.
emirate-of-bohtan.o: The Azizan family, which claimed descent from the Arab general Khalid ibn al-Walid, ruled Jazirat ibn Umar (Cizre) and the Bohtan region on the Tigris from the late Middle Ages, their power predating the arrival of the Ottomans.
emirate-of-bohtan.r: After 1514 the emirate accepted Ottoman suzerainty and kept hereditary rule. Cizre was a centre of Kurdish learning: the poet Ahmad Khani set his epic Mem u Zin of 1692 at its court. In the 1840s Bedir Khan Beg extended his power across the region, and his forces massacred Assyrian Christians of Hakkari in 1843 and 1846.
emirate-of-bohtan.e: Ottoman troops defeated Bedir Khan in 1847 and exiled him to Crete, ending the emirate. His descendants, the Bedirxan family, became leading Kurdish nationalists, publishing the first Kurdish newspaper, Kurdistan, in 1898.

exarchate-of-ravenna.t: Byzantine province ruling what remained of imperial Italy from Ravenna, under an exarch combining military and civil power, until the Lombards took Ravenna in 751.
exarchate-of-ravenna.o: After the Lombard invasion of 568 broke Byzantine Italy into scattered territories, Emperor Maurice concentrated civil and military authority in a single governor, the exarch, based at Ravenna. The office is first attested in 584. It was a new form of government designed for a frontier under constant attack.
exarchate-of-ravenna.r: The exarch governed Ravenna, the Pentapolis, the Duchy of Rome, Naples, Venetia and other fragments, commanding local garrisons whose officers became a landed aristocracy. Relations with the popes were often tense, especially over Monothelitism and Iconoclasm. Several exarchs rebelled, among them Eleutherius in 619 and Olympius in 649. Ravenna remained a centre of Greek-Latin culture, its churches adorned with mosaics.
exarchate-of-ravenna.e: Lombard pressure grew in the 8th century; King Aistulf captured Ravenna in 751, killing or expelling the last exarch, Eutychius. When Pepin the Short defeated Aistulf, he gave the exarchate's lands to the pope in 756, forming the core of the Papal States.

epidii.t: People of Kintyre in western Scotland recorded by Ptolemy, whose name means 'horse people' and whose land later became the heart of Dál Riata.
epidii.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Epidii in the Kintyre peninsula and neighbouring islands of Argyll, with the Mull of Kintyre named Epidion Akron after them. Their name comes from the Brittonic word for horse, suggesting a people who honoured horses or a horse deity.
epidii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Kintyre and the islands were a land of duns, crannogs and small forts, with the sea as the main highway. The peninsula lies only about 20 kilometres from Antrim, and contact with Ireland was constant across the North Channel.
epidii.e: The Epidii disappear from the record after Ptolemy. By the 6th century their region was ruled by the Gaelic kings of Dál Riata, whose territory spanned Argyll and north Antrim, and Kintyre was held by its leading kindred, the Cenél nGabráin.

empire-of-nicaea.t: The largest Byzantine successor state after 1204, which rebuilt Byzantine power in Anatolia and recaptured Constantinople in 1261.
empire-of-nicaea.o: As the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, Theodore Laskaris, son-in-law of Alexios III, gathered refugees and troops in Bithynia. With Nicaea as his base he fought off the Latins and the Seljuks, and in 1208 had himself crowned emperor by a newly elected patriarch, giving his state the strongest claim to Byzantine legitimacy.
empire-of-nicaea.r: The Laskarid emperors governed through a Byzantine-style court and bureaucracy, with the patriarch residing at Nicaea and the court often at Nymphaion. John III Vatatzes promoted agricultural self-sufficiency, restricted luxury imports, founded charities and expanded into Europe, taking Thessalonica in 1246. Scholarship flourished under Nikephoros Blemmydes and Theodore II Laskaris.
empire-of-nicaea.e: Michael VIII Palaiologos seized power from the boy emperor John IV, defeated the Latins and Epirotes at Pelagonia in 1259 and took Constantinople in July 1261, restoring the Byzantine Empire. Neglect of the Anatolian frontier after the move opened the way to Turkish expansion.

edom.t: Edom, a kingdom of the arid highlands south of the Dead Sea, rich in copper and the incense trade, rival of Judah.
edom.o: The Edomites lived in the mountains east of the Arabah valley, mentioned in Egyptian texts from the 13th century BCE. In the 10th century BCE large-scale copper smelting at Faynan, such as Khirbat en-Nahas, supported an emerging elite, and a kingdom with its capital at Bozrah formed by the 8th century BCE.
edom.r: Edomite kings worshipped the god Qos and drew revenue from copper and from caravan routes carrying Arabian incense to Gaza. The Bible records wars with the Kingdom of Judah. Edom became a loyal vassal of the Assyrian Empire, and kings such as Qaus-gabri sent tribute and workers.
edom.e: Edom survived the fall of Assyria but lost its independence to Nabonidus of the Chaldean Empire, who campaigned there c. 552 BCE. Edomites later settled in southern Judah, which became Idumaea, while Arab groups and the Nabataean Kingdom took their old lands.

eleutherna.t: Hill city of western Crete on the slopes of Mount Ida whose Orthi Petra cemetery has revealed rich warrior burials of the early Iron Age.
eleutherna.o: Eleutherna occupied a long ridge on the north-west slopes of Mount Ida, inhabited since the Bronze Age. It grew into a city in the early Iron Age, and by the 7th century BCE it was one of the important poleis of Crete.
eleutherna.r: Excavations at the Orthi Petra necropolis since 1985 have found rich burials of the 9th to 7th centuries BCE, including warriors and elite women with gold jewellery. Like other Cretan cities, Eleutherna had kosmoi magistrates and aristocratic institutions. It minted coins showing Apollo and took part in Hellenistic alliances and the Cretan Koinon.
eleutherna.e: Metellus captured Eleutherna during the Roman conquest of Crete in 68 or 67 BCE. It continued as a Roman and early Byzantine town before being abandoned, probably after an earthquake in the 7th century CE.

earldom-of-bamburgh.t: The English lordship that survived the Viking conquest of York, ruling northern Northumbria from the fortress of Bamburgh.
earldom-of-bamburgh.o: When the Great Heathen Army took York in 867, the northern part of the Kingdom of Northumbria between the Tees and the Tweed remained under English rulers based at Bamburgh. Its leaders, such as Eadwulf and his descendants, styled themselves high-reeves or even kings of the northern English.
earldom-of-bamburgh.r: Bamburgh's lords protected the community of Saint Cuthbert, which moved with its relics to Chester-le-Street and then Durham. They recognised West Saxon kings from Aethelstan onwards, while defending Lothian against Scottish attack. Uhtred the Bold defeated the Scots at Durham in 1006 and held the whole earldom of Northumbria.
earldom-of-bamburgh.e: Feuds and Danish rule weakened the house. In 1041 Earl Siward killed Eadwulf, the last of the line, and united Northumbria under his own authority as part of the Kingdom of England. Lothian had already passed to the Kingdom of Scotland.

earldom-of-desmond.t: The FitzGerald lordship of Munster that became more Gaelic than the Gaels, destroyed in the Desmond Rebellions of the 1570s and 1580s.
earldom-of-desmond.o: The FitzGeralds descended from Maurice FitzGerald, one of the first Cambro-Norman invaders of 1169. Maurice FitzThomas FitzGerald was created Earl of Desmond in 1329 with palatine rights over Kerry.
earldom-of-desmond.r: The Desmond earls ruled much of Munster from castles such as Askeaton and Newcastle West, adopting Irish language, law and patronage of poets. Gerald, the 3rd Earl, was a noted Irish poet. They were often at odds with the Butler earls of the Earldom of Ormond and with the Dublin government.
earldom-of-desmond.e: Gerald FitzGerald, the 15th Earl, rebelled against Elizabeth I in the Desmond Rebellions. He was killed in 1583, and his vast lands were confiscated and granted to English settlers in the Plantation of Munster.

eastern-guo.t: A Ji-clan state near Xingyang founded by a brother of King Wen of Zhou and swallowed by the newly arrived State of Zheng in 767 BCE.
eastern-guo.o: Eastern Guo was established early in the Western Zhou by Guo Shu or Guo Zhong, younger brothers of King Wen, whose descendants held two separate Guo states. The eastern one, centred at Zhi near modern Xingyang in Henan, guarded the approaches to the eastern capital at Luoyi.
eastern-guo.r: Its rulers were close kin of the Zhou kings and held the rank of duke, but little else is known of their government. The state controlled strategic ground near the Yellow River and the Xingyang pass.
eastern-guo.e: When the Zhou court moved east in 770 BCE, Duke Huan of Zheng had already deposited his family and treasure with Eastern Guo and nearby Kuai. His son Duke Wu of Zheng conquered Eastern Guo in 767 BCE, and the State of Zheng built its power on its lands.

erivan-khanate.t: The Persian-ruled khanate around Yerevan and the Ararat plain, whose conquest by Russia in 1827-1828 began modern Armenia's territorial history.
erivan-khanate.o: The Erivan province had been an Iranian administrative unit since Safavid times. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747, its governors acted as autonomous khans of the Ararat plain and the area around Lake Sevan, while recognising Persian overlordship whenever a strong shah ruled.
erivan-khanate.r: The khans ruled from the fortress of Erivan over a mixed population of Muslims and Armenians, with Etchmiadzin, seat of the Armenian Catholicos, within the khanate. Irrigated farming of cotton, rice and fruit sustained it. The khanate paid tribute to the Zand Empire and to Erekle II of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti before Qajar Iran restored control. Hosein Qoli Khan Qajar, governor from 1807, built the Sardar's Palace.
erivan-khanate.e: Russian troops under Ivan Paskevich captured Erivan in 1827, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 ceded the khanate to the Russian Empire. Combined with Nakhichevan, it became the Armenian Oblast, and many Armenians from Iran settled there.

emirate-of-granada.t: The last Muslim state in Iberia, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty for over 250 years and builder of the Alhambra.
emirate-of-granada.o: In 1232 Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr, known as Ibn al-Ahmar, proclaimed himself ruler at Arjona amid the collapse of Almohad power. He took Granada in 1237-1238 and in 1246 accepted vassalage to Ferdinand III of Castile, ceding Jaén and paying tribute to survive.
emirate-of-granada.r: The emirate covered the mountains and coasts from Almería to Gibraltar, dense with refugees from lost Andalusi cities. Silk, sugar and dried fruit were exported through Málaga, often by Genoese merchants. Yusuf I and Muhammad V built the finest parts of the Alhambra, and poets such as Ibn Zamrak and the vizier Ibn al-Khatib served the court.
emirate-of-granada.e: Weakened by dynastic feuds, Granada fell in the war of 1482-1492. Muhammad XII, Boabdil, surrendered the city to Isabella I and Ferdinand II on 2 January 1492. Its Muslims later faced forced conversion and, as Moriscos, expulsion.

edetani.t: An Iberian people of the Valencian plain, centred on Edeta near Llíria, whose leader Edeco was among the first to join Rome.
edetani.o: The Edetani occupied the coastal plain and hills of the modern province of Valencia, between the Júcar and the Mijares, from about the 5th century BCE. Their capital, Edeta, stood on the hill of Tossal de Sant Miquel above Llíria.
edetani.r: Edeta's excavated houses have yielded famous painted pottery showing warriors, dancers and hunting scenes, with Iberian inscriptions. The Edetani lived from farming, crafts and trade along the coast, and their leaders controlled networks of villages and watchtowers. In 209 BCE their prince Edeco went over to Scipio after the fall of Carthago Nova, recovering his family held hostage there.
edetani.e: The Edetani joined Rome during the Second Punic War and were absorbed into Hispania Citerior. In 138 BCE the Romans founded Valentia, modern Valencia, in their territory, and Edeta itself was later abandoned in favour of a Roman town on the plain.

electorate-of-bavaria.t: Bavaria as one of the great electoral principalities of the Empire, a Catholic power whose dukes twice sought the imperial crown.
electorate-of-bavaria.o: Duke Maximilian I, head of the Catholic League, helped crush the Bohemian revolt at the White Mountain in 1620. As a reward Emperor Ferdinand II transferred the electoral dignity of the Palatinate to him in 1623, together with the Upper Palatinate, confirmed at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
electorate-of-bavaria.r: The electorate was firmly Catholic, with strong ties to the Jesuits and a rich baroque church culture. The electors built Nymphenburg and Schleissheim palaces in and near Munich. Max Emanuel allied with France in the War of the Spanish Succession and lost his lands after Blenheim in 1704, and Charles Albert was elected Emperor Charles VII in 1742 during the Austrian Succession war.
electorate-of-bavaria.e: In 1777 the Bavarian Wittelsbachs died out and the electorate passed to Charles Theodore of the Palatinate. Allied with Napoleon, Elector Maximilian IV Joseph gained large territories and became King of Bavaria on 1 January 1806.

emirate-of-tarsus.t: The great frontier fortress of Cilicia, a base for holy war against Byzantium that drew volunteer fighters from across the Islamic world.
emirate-of-tarsus.o: Tarsus lay abandoned in the frontier zone until the Abbasids rebuilt and garrisoned it in the late 8th century, a project completed under Harun al-Rashid. It became the chief city of the Cilician thughur, the line of fortified towns on the Byzantine border.
emirate-of-tarsus.r: The city was governed by appointees of Baghdad and later of the Tulunids, Ikhshidids and Hamdanids, but its garrison and civic leaders acted largely independently. Volunteers came from Khurasan, Iraq and Egypt to live in ribats, fortified hostels, and join the annual raids. Commanders such as Yazaman al-Khadim and Thamal al-Dulafi led land and naval raids into Anatolia and the Aegean, and prisoner exchanges with Byzantium were held on the nearby Lamos river.
emirate-of-tarsus.e: In 965 the Byzantine emperor Nikephoros II Phokas captured Tarsus after a long blockade. Its Muslim inhabitants were allowed to leave and the city was resettled with Christians, ending three centuries of Muslim rule in Cilicia.

epirote-league.t: Federal republic of the peoples of Epirus that replaced the Aeacid monarchy and ended in mass enslavement by Rome in 167 BCE.
epirote-league.o: Around 232 BCE the last of the royal Aeacid family, Deidamia, was killed and the Molossians, Chaonians and Thesprotians abolished the monarchy of the Kingdom of Epirus. They formed a federal state, the Koinon of the Epirotes, whose meetings were often held at Phoenice in Chaonia, near the Ionian coast.
epirote-league.r: The league was led by annually elected generals and a federal assembly, and minted coins showing Zeus and Dione of Dodona. Its regions remained distinct, and wealth came from herding and trade with Italy. Illyrian raiders under Queen Teuta sacked Phoenice in 230 BCE. The Peace of Phoenice, ending the First Macedonian War in 205 BCE, was signed there.
epirote-league.e: In the Third Macedonian War the Molossians sided with Perseus while other Epirotes supported Rome. In 167 BCE the Roman Senate ordered Lucius Aemilius Paullus to punish Epirus: seventy towns were plundered and about 150,000 people enslaved, ending the league.
epirote-league.re: Ancient Greek religion (cult of Zeus at Dodona)

elisu-sultanate.t: A small Tsakhur sultanate in the foothills of north-western Azerbaijan whose last sultan defected from Russia to join Imam Shamil.
elisu-sultanate.o: The Elisu Sultanate took shape around 1604 among the Tsakhur people of the southern slopes of the Caucasus, centred on the village of Ilisu. Its rulers, who took the title sultan, emerged as the Safavid Empire reasserted control over the region after wars with the Ottomans.
elisu-sultanate.r: The sultans ruled Tsakhur, Azerbaijani and Georgian-speaking Ingiloy villages, collecting tribute and leading raids into Kakheti. The land lived by herding, orchards and silk. Its rulers balanced between the Safavid Empire, the khanates of Shaki and Shirvan, the Lezgin free communities of Jar and Belokan and later Russia.
elisu-sultanate.e: The sultanate accepted Russian protection in 1803. In 1844 Sultan Daniyal Bek, though a Russian major general, joined Imam Shamil's Caucasian Imamate, and the Russian Empire abolished the sultanate. Daniyal Bek became one of Shamil's naibs and later made peace with Russia.

emirate-of-diriyah.t: The first Saudi state, born of an alliance between the Al Saud and the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, which conquered most of Arabia.
emirate-of-diriyah.o: Muhammad ibn Saud became emir of the small oasis town of Diriyah in Najd in 1727. In 1744 he made a pact with Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, a preacher calling for a return to strict monotheism: the Al Saud would support the reform movement, and the scholar would legitimise their rule.
emirate-of-diriyah.r: The emirate expanded by war and conversion, taking Riyadh in 1773, defeating the Banu Khalid Emirate and conquering al-Hasa. It collected zakat from subject towns and tribes and destroyed shrines seen as idolatrous. Under Saud ibn Abd al-Aziz its forces sacked Karbala in 1802 and took Mecca in 1803 and Medina soon after, and raided Iraq, Syria and Oman.
emirate-of-diriyah.e: The Ottoman Empire sent the army of Egypt under Muhammad Ali. Ibrahim Pasha besieged and destroyed Diriyah in 1818; the last emir, Abdullah ibn Saud, was executed in Istanbul. The Emirate of Nejd revived Saudi rule in 1824. The ruins of al-Turaif are a World Heritage Site.

emirate-of-chefchaouen.t: A mountain emirate in the Rif founded as a base for holy war against Portuguese Ceuta, a refuge for exiles from Granada.
emirate-of-chefchaouen.o: Chefchaouen was founded in 1471 by Ali ibn Rashid, a sharif of the Banu Rashid, as a fortified base for raids against the Portuguese enclaves of Portuguese Morocco around Ceuta and Ksar es-Seghir. Muslim and Jewish refugees from Granada swelled the town after 1492.
emirate-of-chefchaouen.r: The emirs ruled the western Rif and Jbala hills semi-independently, nominally recognising the Wattasid Sultanate in Fez. Andalusi settlers gave the town its whitewashed houses and craft traditions. Ali's daughter Sayyida al-Hurra married the lord of Tetouan and later governed that city herself, linking the two states.
emirate-of-chefchaouen.e: The Saadi Sultanate subdued the emirate around 1561, ending Banu Rashid rule. Chefchaouen remained a closed holy town, rarely visited by Europeans before the 20th century, and is today a well-known Moroccan city.

ekron.t: Ekron, a Philistine city that grew into the largest olive-oil producer of the ancient Near East under Assyrian rule.
ekron.o: Ekron, at Tel Miqne, was refounded in the 12th century BCE by newcomers whose pottery, hearths and diet show roots in the Aegean world. They built a planned town that formed one of the five cities of the Philistine Pentapolis.
ekron.r: Ekron shrank in the 10th century BCE, then boomed in the 7th as a vassal of the Assyrian Empire, with over a hundred olive presses producing oil for export. A dedication inscription found in 1996 names Ikausu son of Padi as king and the goddess Ptgyh, confirming the city's identity.
ekron.e: In 701 BCE Padi was handed to Hezekiah of the Kingdom of Judah by rebels, then restored by Sennacherib. Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire destroyed Ekron in 604 BCE, ending the city.

emirate-of-kish.t: A seafaring island emirate in the Persian Gulf that dominated trade between Iraq, India and Arabia in the 12th century.
emirate-of-kish.o: As the port of Siraf declined after its 10th-century earthquake, merchants and sea captains on the island of Kish, called Qays in Arabic, took over its trade. By around 1100 a local dynasty, the Banu Qaysar, ruled an independent emirate there.
emirate-of-kish.r: Kish lived from maritime commerce and from levying ships passing through the Gulf, and it maintained a fleet that raided rival ports and even attacked Aden in 1135. It controlled the pearl fisheries and at times the Bahrain islands. Geographers such as Yaqut describe its markets and its rulers' wealth, but its internal history is poorly recorded.
emirate-of-kish.e: In 1229 the island was conquered by the Salghurid atabegs of Fars with help from the Kingdom of Ormus, which then inherited much of its trade.

etruscan-league.t: Federation of twelve Etruscan city-states that met yearly at the sanctuary of Voltumna, more a religious union than a military alliance.
etruscan-league.o: By the 6th century BCE the leading cities of Etruria formed a group known to the Romans as the twelve peoples of Etruria. Its focus was the Fanum Voltumnae, a federal sanctuary near Volsinii, possibly at Campo della Fiera below Orvieto, where delegates met each spring.
etruscan-league.r: The list of members changed over time but usually included Veii, Caere, Tarquinii, Vulci, Volsinii, Clusium, Perusia, Cortona, Arretium, Volaterrae, Vetulonia or Rusellae, and Populonia. The annual gathering combined sacrifices, games and markets with political councils, and chose a federal leader whose powers were mainly ceremonial. It rarely acted together in war: Livy says it refused to help Veii against Rome.
etruscan-league.e: As Rome conquered the Etruscan cities one by one, the League lost all political weight, ending with the destruction of Volsinii in 264 BCE. Under the Empire a ceremonial league of fifteen peoples was revived with a praetor of Etruria, and the festival was still held in the 4th century CE.

electoral-palatinate.t: The Rhineland electorate of the Wittelsbach counts palatine, centre of German Calvinism, whose elector's Bohemian adventure began the Thirty Years' War.
electoral-palatinate.o: The counts palatine of Lotharingia, royal deputies in the Rhineland, moved their power to the middle Rhine; around 1085 to 1087 Henry of Laach is first called count palatine of the Rhine. Under the Staufer and from 1214 the Wittelsbachs, the Palatinate grew around Heidelberg, Alzey and the upper Rhine.
electoral-palatinate.r: The Golden Bull of 1356 made the count palatine an elector and imperial vicar. Rupert I founded the University of Heidelberg in 1386, and Rupert III became King of the Romans in 1400. Elector Frederick III adopted Calvinism and sponsored the Heidelberg Catechism of 1563, making the Palatinate the leading Reformed state of the Empire.
electoral-palatinate.e: Frederick V accepted the Bohemian crown in 1619 and lost his lands and electoral vote. The Palatinate was devastated in the Thirty Years' War and again by France in 1689. France annexed the left bank in 1797, and in 1803 the remaining lands went to Baden and others.

euboean-league.t: Federation of the cities of Euboea, born from the island's revolt against Athens in 411 BCE and revived repeatedly under Macedonian and Roman patrons.
euboean-league.o: Euboea was vital to Athens, supplying food and pasture. In 411 BCE, after a Spartan naval victory off Eretria, its cities revolted and formed a league, building a bridge across the Euripus to link Chalcis with the mainland. Federal coins inscribed for the Euboeans appear from about this time.
euboean-league.r: The league joined Chalcis, Eretria, Histiaea and Carystus with a federal council and coinage, though the larger cities often pursued their own policies. Its history was one of shifting allegiances: members joined the Second Athenian League, while Callias of Chalcis revived the federation in the 340s BCE in a contest between Athens and Philip II for the island.
euboean-league.e: Under the Hellenistic kings, Chalcis was one of Macedon's 'fetters of Greece'. After Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks in 196 BCE the league was refounded under Roman patronage. It lost its independence after the Achaean War of 146 BCE, when Chalcis was punished for supporting the Achaeans.

eastern-kara-khanid-khanate.t: The eastern branch of the Kara-Khanid dynasty, ruling Kashgar and the Tarim cities, where Mahmud al-Kashgari and Yusuf Balasaguni wrote their classics.
eastern-kara-khanid-khanate.o: Around 1042 the Kara-Khanid Khanate split into two rival branches. The eastern khanate, under the descendants of Ali ibn Musa, held Kashgar, Balasagun, the Ili valley and the western Tarim, while the Western Kara-Khanid Khanate held Transoxiana.
eastern-kara-khanid-khanate.r: The eastern khans ruled Turkic tribes and oasis towns, continuing the work of converting the Tarim Basin to Islam, including wars with the Buddhist Kingdom of Khotan earlier and with the Kingdom of Qocho. Kashgar became a centre of Turkic Islamic culture: Yusuf Balasaguni presented his mirror for princes, the Kutadgu Bilig, to the Kashgar khan around 1069.
eastern-kara-khanid-khanate.e: In the 1130s the Qara Khitai took Balasagun and reduced the eastern khans to vassals ruling Kashgar. The last khan, Muhammad, was killed in 1211 by Kuchlug, the Naiman prince who had seized the Qara Khitai throne, shortly before the Mongol conquest.

eshrefids.t: A short-lived beylik on Lake Beysehir whose wooden-columned Eshrefoglu Mosque is a World Heritage Site.
eshrefids.o: The Eshrefids descended from Eshref, a Turkmen commander serving the Sultanate of Rum. In the 1280s Sayf al-Din Suleyman Bey made Beysehir on the lake of the same name the centre of a principality as Seljuk power waned.
eshrefids.r: The beylik held Beysehir, Seydisehir and Aksehir at times. Suleyman Bey built the Eshrefoglu Mosque in 1296-1299, whose interior has a forest of carved cedar columns and painted wooden ceilings, among the finest surviving wooden mosques; it was listed with other Anatolian wooden mosques as a World Heritage Site in 2023. The beylik had little political weight among its neighbours.
eshrefids.e: In 1326 the Ilkhanid governor of Anatolia, Timurtash, executed its last ruler, Suleyman II, and the lands passed to the Hamidids.

electorate-of-saxony.t: The Wettin electorate on the Elbe that cradled the Lutheran Reformation and, under Augustus the Strong, made Dresden a Baroque capital.
electorate-of-saxony.o: The Golden Bull of 1356 made the Ascanian dukes of the Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg prince-electors. When their line ended in 1422, Emperor Sigismund granted the electorate to Frederick the Warlike, Margrave of Meissen, joining it to the Wettin lands of Meissen and Thuringia. In 1485 the brothers Ernest and Albert divided these lands, and the electoral dignity went to the Ernestine line.
electorate-of-saxony.r: Silver mining in the Erzgebirge made Saxony rich. Elector Frederick the Wise founded Wittenberg University and protected Martin Luther, and Saxony became the leading Lutheran state. After the Schmalkaldic War of 1547 the electorate passed to the Albertine Maurice, with Dresden as capital. Augustus the Strong, king of Poland from 1697, built the Zwinger and founded the Meissen porcelain works.
electorate-of-saxony.e: Saxony was badly weakened by Prussia in the Seven Years' War. Allied with Napoleon, Elector Frederick Augustus III took the title of king in 1806, turning the electorate into the Kingdom of Saxony, which lost much of its territory to Prussia in 1815.

earldom-of-lade.t: Dynasty of earls based near Trondheim who rivalled the descendants of Harald Fairhair and ruled Norway for long periods around 1000.
earldom-of-lade.o: The earls took their name from Lade, a farm near modern Trondheim in Trøndelag. Håkon Grjotgardsson, whose family came from Hålogaland, allied with Harald Fairhair in the late 9th century and was made earl of the Trøndelag region, founding a powerful line.
earldom-of-lade.r: The jarls of Lade drew strength from the rich farming districts and assemblies of Trøndelag and from the northern fur trade. Håkon Sigurdsson, known as Haakon Jarl, ruled most of Norway from about 975 to 995 under the overlordship of Harald Bluetooth of Denmark and was a champion of the pagan cults. After the Battle of Svolder in 1000, his sons Eric and Sweyn governed Norway for the kings of Denmark and Sweden.
earldom-of-lade.e: Olaf Haraldsson drove out the earls in 1015. Cnut the Great restored Håkon Eiriksson as his regent in Norway in 1028, but Håkon drowned around 1030 and the line ended. Trøndelag passed fully to the Kingdom of Norway, and Trondheim (Nidaros) became its religious centre.

emirate-of-derbent.t: An Arab frontier emirate at the great Caspian gate of Derbent, guarding Islam's northern border against the Khazars and mountain peoples.
emirate-of-derbent.o: Derbent, called Bab al-Abwab, the Gate of Gates, by the Arabs, had been fortified by the Sasanians with walls running from the Caspian into the mountains. In 869, as Abbasid authority faded, the local Arab governor Hashim ibn Suraqa founded a hereditary dynasty, the Hashimids.
emirate-of-derbent.r: The emirate was a frontier city-state that drew warriors for holy war against the Khazar Khaganate and the peoples of the mountains, and grew rich on Caspian and caravan trade in slaves, furs and textiles. Emirs shared power with an assembly of leading citizens and often fought or allied with the Shirvanshah State, which at times ruled the city.
emirate-of-derbent.e: Weakened by quarrels between emirs and townsmen and by raids from the mountains, the emirate was taken by the Seljuk Empire in 1075. The city later passed among regional powers, keeping its walls as the gateway to the North Caucasus.

esuvii.t: Little-known Gallic people of lower Normandy subdued by Caesar's legate Crassus during the conquest of Armorica.
esuvii.o: Caesar mentions the Esuvii among the Armorican peoples brought under Roman control by Publius Crassus in 57 BCE, and notes that a legion wintered in their territory in 54 BCE. Their exact location is debated, but most scholars place them in the Orne region around Sées or Exmes.
esuvii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions; their name may be linked to the Gallic god Esus.
esuvii.e: After the conquest they disappear from the record, and their land seems to have been absorbed into the civitas of the Sagii, whose town became Sées.

epidaurus.t: Argolid city-state whose sanctuary of Asclepius became the most famous healing centre of the Greek world, with its magnificent theatre.
epidaurus.o: Epidaurus lay on a small peninsula on the east coast of the Argolid. In the early Iron Age Dorian settlers from Argos made it an independent city; tradition held that Epidaurians in turn settled Aegina. Its sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas inland gradually gave way to the cult of his son Asclepius.
epidaurus.r: Epidaurus was governed by an oligarchy of 180 citizens. From the late 5th century BCE the Asclepieion attracted sick pilgrims who slept in the sanctuary hoping for healing dreams, and inscriptions record their cures. The 4th century BCE theatre, attributed to Polykleitos the Younger, seats about 13,000. Epidaurus was a loyal member of the Peloponnesian League.
epidaurus.e: Epidaurus joined the Achaean League in 243 BCE and passed under Rome in 146 BCE. Sulla plundered the sanctuary in 87 BCE, but it recovered and flourished in Roman times; its theatre still hosts performances.
