emirate-of-nejd-and-hasa.t: The third Saudi state in its first phase, begun when Ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh in 1902, which defeated the Rashidis and took al-Hasa.
emirate-of-nejd-and-hasa.o: In January 1902 the young Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, living in exile in the Sheikhdom of Kuwait, captured Riyadh's Masmak fort from the Rashidi governor with a small band of followers. He gradually reclaimed southern Najd from the Emirate of Jabal Shammar, defeating its emir at Rawdat Muhanna in 1906.
emirate-of-nejd-and-hasa.r: Ibn Saud combined tribal diplomacy, marriage alliances and the Wahhabi religious establishment. From about 1912 he settled Bedouin in agricultural communities called hijras, creating the Ikhwan, a militant religious force. In 1913 he took al-Hasa from the Ottoman Empire, gaining the Gulf coast. The Treaty of Darin in 1915 made him a British protégé with a subsidy.
emirate-of-nejd-and-hasa.e: In 1921 Ibn Saud conquered Ha'il, ending the Rashidi state, and took the title Sultan of Nejd and its Dependencies, beginning the Sultanate of Nejd.

eretnids.t: The successor state to Mongol rule in central Anatolia, founded by an Uyghur officer who made himself sultan in Sivas and Kayseri.
eretnids.o: Eretna was an Uyghur commander who served the Ilkhanid governor of Anatolia, Timurtash. After the death of the last strong Ilkhan, Abu Sa'id, in 1335, he governed central Anatolia on his own account, first in the name of rival Mongol princes and from 1341 as sultan, minting coins in his own name.
eretnids.r: In 1343 Eretna defeated a Chobanid army at Karanbuk, securing his state. His realm included Sivas, Kayseri, Tokat, Amasya and Erzincan, with a Mongol and Turkmen military elite and Persian administration in the Seljuk tradition. After his death in 1352 his son Mehmed and grandson Ala al-Din Ali faced revolts by emirs and Turkmen chiefs.
eretnids.e: Real power passed to the vizier and judge Kadi Burhan al-Din, who after Ala al-Din Ali's death in 1380 took the throne in 1381, ending the dynasty.

electorate-of-wurttemberg.t: Württemberg's brief rank as an electorate between the duchy and the kingdom, a step in Frederick I's rise under Napoleon.
electorate-of-wurttemberg.o: Duke Frederick II of Württemberg lost his lands at Montbéliard to France but gained secularised church lands and imperial cities in the Imperial Recess of 1803. As part of the same settlement he was made an elector of the Holy Roman Empire.
electorate-of-wurttemberg.r: Frederick used his new rank to centralise power, overriding the traditional estates, which had long limited the dukes. He added former imperial cities such as Heilbronn and Reutlingen and Catholic lands like Ellwangen, which made the Protestant state more mixed in religion. He allied with Napoleon in 1805 and sent troops to the Austerlitz campaign.
electorate-of-wurttemberg.e: The Peace of Pressburg rewarded Frederick with further territory and recognition as a sovereign king. On 1 January 1806 he proclaimed himself King of Württemberg, and the electorate gave way to the Kingdom of Württemberg.

ebla.t: Ebla, a Bronze Age kingdom in northern Syria whose palace archive of thousands of clay tablets revealed an early Semitic state rivalling Mari and Mesopotamia.
ebla.o: Ebla grew from a settlement at Tell Mardikh, south-west of modern Aleppo, into a walled city by the middle of the 3rd millennium BCE. By c. 2400 BCE it controlled a large territory of farming villages and pasture in western Syria and dealt as an equal with Mari, Nagar and distant powers along the Euphrates.
ebla.r: Its kings governed with a council of elders and powerful officials such as the vizier Ibrium, recorded in the archive of Palace G, found by Italian excavators under Paolo Matthiae in 1974 and 1975. The tablets, in Sumerian cuneiform and the Semitic Eblaite language, record textiles, metals, flocks of sheep, treaties and offerings to gods such as Kura and Hadda.
ebla.e: Palace G burned c. 2300 BCE, probably at the hands of Sargon or Naram-Sin of the Akkadian Empire. Ebla revived twice, the last time as an Amorite city allied to Yamhad, until a Hittite king destroyed it c. 1600 BCE. Its archive remains one of the oldest bodies of written Semitic texts.

emirate-of-erzincan.t: The principality of Mutahharten, lord of Erzincan, an ally of Timur on the upper Euphrates.
emirate-of-erzincan.o: Mutahharten was a governor of Erzincan under the Eretnids. As that dynasty collapsed in the late 1370s, he made the city and its fertile plain an independent emirate, competing with Kadi Burhan al-Din of Sivas.
emirate-of-erzincan.r: Mutahharten ruled a mixed population of Turks, Armenians and Greeks and kept close ties with the Empire of Trebizond. Threatened by Kadi Burhan al-Din and by Bayezid I, he accepted Timur's overlordship and helped provoke the conflict between Timur and the Ottomans. The Castilian envoy Ruy Gonzalez de Clavijo passed through Erzincan in 1404 on his way to Samarkand.
emirate-of-erzincan.e: Mutahharten died around 1403. His successors could not hold out, and the Qara Qoyunlu took Erzincan in 1410.

emirate-of-jabal-shammar.t: The Rashidi emirate of Ha'il, which overthrew the second Saudi state and dominated northern Arabia before losing to Ibn Saud.
emirate-of-jabal-shammar.o: In 1836 Abdullah ibn Rashid took control of Ha'il, the main town of the Jabal Shammar mountains, with the backing of the Saudi ruler Faisal ibn Turki. His family, leaders of the Shammar tribal confederation, at first ruled as allies of the Emirate of Nejd.
emirate-of-jabal-shammar.r: Ha'il prospered on the pilgrim route from Iraq and Persia to Mecca and on the camel and horse trade. Talal ibn Rashid encouraged merchants and building. Muhammad ibn Rashid, emir from 1869 to 1897, intervened in the Saudi civil war, took Riyadh in 1887 and won at Mulayda in 1891, becoming master of central Arabia. The Rashidis allied with the Ottoman Empire.
emirate-of-jabal-shammar.e: Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh in 1902 and the Emirate of Nejd and Hasa steadily pushed back the Rashidis, killing Abd al-Aziz ibn Mutib in 1906. Weakened by assassinations and the Ottoman defeat, Ha'il surrendered to Ibn Saud in 1921 and joined the Sultanate of Nejd.

emporion.t: The Greek trading city of Empúries in Catalonia, founded from Massalia, where the Romans first landed in Iberia in 218 BCE.
emporion.o: Around 575 BCE Phocaean Greeks from Massalia (Marseille) set up a trading post on a small island at the mouth of the Fluvià, now Sant Martí d'Empúries. Its name means 'market'. A larger new town, the Neapolis, soon grew on the mainland shore beside a native settlement of the Indigetes.
emporion.r: Emporion was a self-governing Greek polis trading wine, oil and fine pottery for grain, metals and textiles from the Iberian interior. It coexisted closely with its Indigetan neighbours, and from the 5th century BCE minted silver drachms, later with a Pegasus design that Iberian mints copied. Strabo notes a temple of Ephesian Artemis, and a famous statue of Asclepius was found in its sanctuary.
emporion.e: Allied with Rome, Emporion was the landing point of Gnaeus Scipio in 218 BCE and of Cato in 195 BCE, when he crushed the revolt of the north-east. A Roman town grew beside it, and under Augustus the two merged as the municipium of Emporiae.

eldiguzids.t: A Turkic dynasty of atabegs who, from Nakhchivan and Tabriz, controlled the late Seljuk sultans and dominated north-western Iran and Arran.
eldiguzids.o: Shams al-Din Eldiguz, a former Kipchak slave, rose in the service of the Seljuks and around 1136 was made governor of Arran and atabeg, or guardian, of the prince Arslan Shah. After placing Arslan Shah on the throne of the Seljuk Sultanate of Iraq in 1160, he became the real power behind it.
eldiguzids.r: The atabegs ruled Azerbaijan, Arran and much of western Iran from Nakhchivan, Tabriz and Hamadan, making and unmaking sultans. Jahan Pahlavan and Qizil Arslan continued their father's dominance. Their court patronised Persian poetry, including Nizami Ganjavi, and the architect Ajami Nakhchivani built the Momine Khatun mausoleum in Nakhchivan in 1186.
eldiguzids.e: The Kingdom of Georgia defeated the atabeg Abu Bakr at Shamkor in 1195, and Mongol raids further weakened Uzbek, the last ruler. In 1225 Jalal al-Din of the Khwarazmian Empire took Tabriz, ending the dynasty.

elusates.t: Aquitanian people of the Armagnac whose town Elusa, modern Eauze, became a provincial capital of late Roman Gaul.
elusates.o: The Elusates lived in the north-west of the modern Gers, in the Armagnac hills. Caesar names them among the Aquitanian peoples who surrendered to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE.
elusates.r: Nothing is known of their pre-Roman government. They belonged to the Aquitani, whose language was related to Basque.
elusates.e: Under Rome Elusa grew into a prosperous town, and in the late 3rd century it became the capital of the province of Novempopulana. The Eauze treasure, a hoard of nearly 28,000 coins and jewellery buried in the 3rd century, shows its wealth.

elea.t: Greek city on the Cilento coast founded by refugees from Phocaea, home of the philosophers Parmenides and Zeno and of the Eleatic school.
elea.o: Around 540 BCE Phocaean Greeks, who had fled their city in Asia Minor before the Persians and then lost much of their fleet at the battle of Alalia off Corsica, founded Elea (later Roman Velia) on a headland south of Poseidonia with help from Rhegion.
elea.r: Elea lived by the sea: fishing, trade and shipping rather than farming, as its hilly territory was poor. It is best known for philosophy: Parmenides, said to have written the city's laws, and his pupil Zeno founded the Eleatic school, which shaped Greek thinking about being and change. The Porta Rosa, a 4th-century BCE arched gateway, is an early true arch in a Greek city. Elea resisted Lucanian pressure while other Greek cities fell.
elea.e: Elea allied with Rome in the early 3rd century BCE and supplied ships in the Punic Wars; Rome recruited priestesses of Ceres from Velia. It kept Greek speech and became a Roman municipium after 89 BCE. Silting of its harbour led to decline, and its remains are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

emirate-of-sicily.t: Muslim Sicily, ruled from Palermo for over two centuries, which transformed the island's farming, cities and language before the Norman conquest.
emirate-of-sicily.o: In 827 the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya invaded Sicily at the invitation of the rebel Byzantine commander Euphemius. Palermo fell in 831 and became the capital, but the conquest was slow: Syracuse fell in 878, Taormina in 902 and Rometta in 965. Malta was taken in 870.
emirate-of-sicily.r: After Fatimid takeover in 909, the Kalbid family ruled as emirs from 948, beginning with Hasan al-Kalbi. Palermo grew into one of the largest Mediterranean cities; Ibn Hawqal counted some 300 mosques. The Arabs introduced citrus, sugar cane, cotton and new irrigation techniques. Christians and Jews lived as protected subjects, and Siculo-Arabic, the ancestor of Maltese, spread widely.
emirate-of-sicily.e: From the 1040s the emirate split among rival lords. One of them, Ibn al-Thumna, invited the Normans, and Roger I took Messina in 1061 and Palermo in 1072; Noto, the last Muslim stronghold, fell in 1091. Arab-Norman culture flourished under the Norman kings.

emirate-of-melitene.t: A Muslim frontier emirate at Malatya on the upper Euphrates that waged two centuries of raiding warfare against Byzantium.
emirate-of-melitene.o: Melitene was taken by the Arabs in the 7th century and changed hands repeatedly. In the 750s the Abbasids resettled and refortified it as a key fortress of the thughur, the frontier zone facing Byzantium, and over time its governors, drawn from the local Arab tribe of Sulaym, became a hereditary dynasty only loosely bound to Baghdad.
emirate-of-melitene.r: The emirate lived by war. Its garrison and volunteer fighters launched seasonal raids across the Taurus into Byzantine Anatolia. Its most famous ruler, Umar al-Aqta, raided deep into Asia Minor, allied with the Paulicians of Tephrike and in 863 sacked Amisos on the Black Sea before being killed at the battle of Lalakaon. The town also had a large Christian population and Syriac monasteries.
emirate-of-melitene.e: As Byzantium went on the offensive in the 10th century, Melitene was repeatedly besieged. In 934 the general John Kourkouas captured it and expelled Muslims who refused to convert, opening the way for Byzantine expansion to the Euphrates.

euesperides.t: The westernmost Greek city of Cyrenaica, on the site of modern Benghazi, later refounded as Berenice.
euesperides.o: Euesperides was founded on the shore of a lagoon near modern Benghazi, probably in the early 6th century BCE, by settlers from the Kingdom of Cyrene. Its name recalls the Garden of the Hesperides, placed nearby by Greek legend. Arcesilaus IV of Cyrene sent new colonists there in the 460s BCE.
euesperides.r: It was a self-governing Greek city with a mixed farming and trading economy, producing grain and olive oil and exporting through its harbour. Excavations have found houses, pottery and coins. Thucydides records that in 414 BCE the Spartan general Gylippus, sailing to Syracuse, helped the city lift a siege by Libyan tribes.
euesperides.e: Euesperides passed to the Ptolemaic Empire in 322 BCE. In the mid-3rd century BCE its population moved to a new site, refounded as Berenice in honour of the wife of Ptolemy III. Berenice later grew into the city of Benghazi.

emirate-of-crete.t: Muslim emirate founded by Andalusian exiles that held Crete for over a century and made it a base for raiding the Byzantine Aegean.
emirate-of-crete.o: After a failed revolt in Cordoba in 818, thousands of Andalusians were expelled from the Umayyad Emirate. Many reached Alexandria, which they held for some years before being forced out. Led by Abu Hafs Umar, they landed on Byzantine Crete in the 820s, conquered the island and founded a fortified capital, Chandax, on the site of modern Heraklion.
emirate-of-crete.r: The emirs ruled as a hereditary dynasty, nominally recognising the Abbasid caliphs, and Arabic and Islam spread among part of the population. The emirate grew rich from raiding Aegean coasts, the slave trade and commerce with Egypt and Syria, and minted its own coins. It repelled several Byzantine expeditions, including those of 843, 911 and 949.
emirate-of-crete.e: In 960 the general Nikephoros Phokas landed a great army and took Chandax after a winter siege in March 961. The last emir, Abd al-Aziz ibn Shu'ayb, was taken to Constantinople. Crete returned to Byzantium and was re-Christianised.

eastern-turkic-khaganate.t: The eastern half of the first Turkic empire, which ruled Mongolia and dominated northern China until Tang Taizong crushed it in 630.
eastern-turkic-khaganate.o: When the First Turkic Khaganate split around 603, the eastern khagans of the Ashina clan held the Mongolian steppe, with their sacred centre at Otuken in the Khangai mountains. The Sui dynasty had encouraged the division, and the khagan Qimin was a Sui ally.
eastern-turkic-khaganate.r: The khagans led a confederation of Turkic and Tiele tribes, extracting silk and tribute from the Chinese states. During the collapse of the Sui, Shibi Khagan besieged Emperor Yang at Yanmen in 615, and his successors backed Chinese rebels and threatened the new Tang dynasty, reaching the Wei River near Chang'an in 626.
eastern-turkic-khaganate.e: Rebellion by the Xueyantuo and other Tiele tribes and a severe winter weakened Illig Khagan, and in 630 a Tang army under Li Jing captured him. The Turks were settled under Tang rule for fifty years until the Second Turkic Khaganate revived their state in 682.

empire-of-trebizond.t: A Byzantine successor state on the Black Sea, ruled by the Grand Komnenoi for over 250 years and the last Byzantine realm to fall.
empire-of-trebizond.o: In April 1204, just before the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople, Alexios and David Komnenos, grandsons of the emperor Andronikos I, seized Trebizond with troops supplied by their relative Queen Tamar of Georgia. Alexios I took the imperial title, founding the dynasty of the Grand Komnenoi.
empire-of-trebizond.r: Trebizond controlled a narrow coastal strip backed by the Pontic mountains and grew rich as a terminus of the trade route from Tabriz, with Venetian and Genoese colonies in the city. Its rulers survived by paying tribute to Seljuks and Mongols and marrying daughters to Turkmen princes, while Alexios III built churches and the Sumela monastery prospered. Greek scholarship flourished; the future cardinal Bessarion was born there.
empire-of-trebizond.e: Mehmed II besieged Trebizond in 1461, eight years after the fall of Constantinople, and the emperor David surrendered in August. He and most of his family were executed in 1463.

emirate-of-hakkari.t: A Kurdish emirate in the mountains south-east of Lake Van, ruling Kurds and Assyrian Christians for nearly five centuries.
emirate-of-hakkari.o: The Hakkari mountains had long been held by Kurdish lords. In the late 14th century a dynasty based at Julamerk (Colemerik) emerged; its emir Izz al-Din Shir submitted to Timur and kept his lands, and his family ruled the region thereafter.
emirate-of-hakkari.r: The emirs ruled a remote mountain land of Kurdish tribes and semi-autonomous Assyrian Christian tribes whose patriarch lived at Qudshanis. After 1514 they became Ottoman vassals with hereditary rule, sometimes switching to the Safavids. Revenues came from flocks, tribute and the roads between Van and Mosul.
emirate-of-hakkari.e: In the 19th century Ottoman centralisation and the revolt of the neighbouring emir Bedir Khan of Bohtan, in which Hakkari's emir Nurullah Bey took part, led to the emirate's abolition in the mid 1840s.

equinoctial-france.t: A short-lived French colony on the island of Maranhão whose fort, Saint-Louis, survives as the city of São Luís in northern Brazil.
equinoctial-france.o: In 1612 an expedition led by Daniel de La Touche, seigneur de La Ravardière, and François de Razilly, with Capuchin friars, landed on the island of Maranhão on Brazil's northern coast. They built Fort Saint-Louis, named after King Louis XIII, and allied with local Tupinambá groups.
equinoctial-france.r: The colony was a small trading and missionary outpost. The Capuchins Claude d'Abbeville and Yves d'Évreux wrote detailed accounts of the Tupinambá, and Abbeville took several Tupinambá to Paris, where they were baptised before the court in 1613. French support from home was weak, and the settlers relied on indigenous allies for food and protection.
equinoctial-france.e: Portugal, then united with Spain, sent forces under Jerónimo de Albuquerque, who defeated the French at Guaxenduba in 1614. La Ravardière surrendered Saint-Louis in 1615. The Portuguese kept the town as São Luís, later capital of the State of Maranhão.

earldom-of-ulster.t: The Anglo-Norman lordship of eastern Ulster founded by John de Courcy and held by the de Burghs, whose collapse in 1333 opened the way to Gaelic recovery.
earldom-of-ulster.o: John de Courcy invaded Ulster in 1177 and ruled it from Carrickfergus and Downpatrick. In 1205 King John expelled him and created the earldom of Ulster for Hugh de Lacy. After de Lacy's death the earldom passed in 1263 to Walter de Burgh.
earldom-of-ulster.r: The earls held coastal Antrim and Down with castles, towns such as Carrickfergus and Coleraine, and manors worked by English settlers. Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl, was the most powerful lord in Ireland around 1300, overlord of the O'Neills and lord of much of Connacht. Edward Bruce's invasion of 1315 to 1318 devastated the earldom.
earldom-of-ulster.e: In 1333 William Donn de Burgh, the Brown Earl, was murdered at Carrickfergus. The earldom passed by marriage to the English royal family, but Gaelic lords such as the O'Neills of Clandeboye reoccupied most of its lands.

electorate-of-hesse.t: Hesse-Kassel as an electorate whose rulers kept the electoral title for sixty years after the Empire ended.
electorate-of-hesse.o: Landgrave William IX of Hesse-Kassel, enriched by hiring out soldiers to Britain, was made an elector in the Imperial Recess of 1803 and took the title Elector William I. The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806 before he could take part in an imperial election.
electorate-of-hesse.r: Napoleon dispossessed William in 1806 and his lands became part of the Kingdom of Westphalia. Restored in 1813, he cancelled the French reforms and kept the title of elector. A constitution was granted in 1831, but Frederick William I quarrelled with his parliament, leading to a crisis in 1850 that nearly brought war between Prussia and Austria. Kassel, the capital, retained the Wilhelmshöhe palace park.
electorate-of-hesse.e: Hesse sided with Austria in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866. Prussia occupied it and annexed it, forming the Province of Hesse-Nassau with the Duchy of Nassau and Frankfurt.

etiuni.t: A confederation of tribes around Lake Sevan and the Ararat plain, whose conquest by Urartu opened the way for the founding of Erebuni, the forerunner of Yerevan.
etiuni.o: Known only from Urartian royal inscriptions. In the 9th century BCE the name Etiuni covered a cluster of tribal lands north of the Araxes, around Lake Sevan and the plain beneath Mount Aragats, which the expanding Kingdom of Urartu treated as one hostile country.
etiuni.r: The union was a loose alliance of local chiefdoms living from cattle herding, farming and bronze and iron working, with hill fortresses of the kind still visible around Sevan. Urartian texts list captured people and livestock in the thousands, showing a populous region but saying little about its institutions.
etiuni.e: Argishti I and Sarduri II of the Kingdom of Urartu conquered Etiuni in a series of campaigns in the early 8th century BCE. Captives were resettled at the new fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BCE, and the region became an Urartian province.

electorate-of-hanover.t: The Brunswick-Lüneburg electorate whose rulers became kings of Great Britain, linking a north German state to a global empire.
electorate-of-hanover.o: Duke Ernest Augustus of Brunswick-Lüneburg, ruling from Hanover, was granted a ninth electoral dignity by Emperor Leopold I in 1692 in return for military support, though it was recognised by the Imperial Diet only in 1708. His wife Sophia was named heir to the British throne by the Act of Settlement of 1701.
electorate-of-hanover.r: In 1714 Sophia's son George Louis became King George I of Great Britain, and Hanover was governed by a privy council while the electors lived mostly in London. The state was Lutheran, agrarian and conservative, run by a nobility-dominated administration. George II founded the University of Göttingen in 1734, which became a leading centre of learning. The Herrenhausen gardens survive from Sophia's time.
electorate-of-hanover.e: Hanover was occupied by France and Prussia in the Napoleonic wars and partly absorbed into the Kingdom of Westphalia. In 1814 the restored state was raised to the Kingdom of Hanover at the Congress of Vienna.

eastern-hungarian-kingdom.t: Rival Hungarian kingdom of John Zápolya and his son, backed by the Ottomans, which became the seed of the Principality of Transylvania.
eastern-hungarian-kingdom.o: After King Louis II died at Mohács in 1526, the Hungarian nobility split. A diet at Székesfehérvár crowned John Zápolya, voivode of Transylvania, in November 1526, while a rival diet chose Ferdinand of Habsburg. Driven out by Ferdinand in 1527, Zápolya accepted the protection of Sultan Suleiman, who restored him to Buda in 1529.
eastern-hungarian-kingdom.r: The kingdom held the eastern half of Hungary and Transylvania under Ottoman suzerainty. After Zápolya's death in 1540, his widow Isabella Jagiellon and the bishop George Martinuzzi governed for the infant John Sigismund. When Suleiman seized Buda in 1541, the court moved to Gyulafehérvár. The Diet of Torda in 1568 proclaimed broad religious freedom.
eastern-hungarian-kingdom.e: By the Treaty of Speyer in 1570, John Sigismund gave up the title of king and was recognised as Prince of Transylvania, turning the realm into the Principality of Transylvania. The division between Habsburg Royal Hungary, Ottoman Hungary and Transylvania lasted until the late 17th century.

emirate-of-transjordan.t: The British-protected emirate of Abdullah east of the Jordan, the forerunner of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.
emirate-of-transjordan.o: After the French expelled his brother Faisal from Damascus, Abdullah, son of Sharif Husayn of Mecca, arrived at Ma'an with followers in late 1920. At the Cairo conference of March 1921 Winston Churchill agreed that he would govern the land east of the Jordan under British mandate, separate from Mandatory Palestine.
emirate-of-transjordan.r: Abdullah built a state from Bedouin tribes and small towns, making Amman his capital. Britain controlled finance and foreign affairs and funded the Arab Legion, built up by Frederick Peake and later John Glubb. The 1922 mandate memorandum excluded Transjordan from the provisions for a Jewish national home. A 1928 treaty and organic law established a legislative council.
emirate-of-transjordan.e: Britain recognised the emirate's independence on 25 May 1946, and Abdullah was proclaimed king of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.

emirate-of-atsiz.t: The first Turkish state in southern Syria and Palestine, carved out by the Turkmen commander Atsiz at the expense of the Fatimids.
emirate-of-atsiz.o: Atsiz ibn Uvaq was a Turkmen commander who entered Fatimid service as Turkish bands spread into Syria after the Seljuk victories. Around 1071 he took Jerusalem and Ramla for himself, and in 1076 he captured Damascus, proclaiming the Abbasid caliph and the Seljuk sultan in Friday prayers.
emirate-of-atsiz.r: His rule rested on Turkmen warriors and was harsh: Damascus suffered famine and extortion, and when Jerusalem rebelled in 1077 he retook it and massacred many inhabitants. In 1077 he invaded Egypt but was defeated near Cairo. His state was a military domain with little administration of its own.
emirate-of-atsiz.e: Threatened by a Fatimid counter-offensive, Atsiz asked Malik-Shah for help. The sultan sent his brother Tutush, who had Atsiz killed in 1079 and took Damascus, founding the Seljuk Sultanate of Syria.

electorate-of-salzburg.t: Short-lived electorate created from the secularised archbishopric of Salzburg for a Habsburg prince who had lost Tuscany.
electorate-of-salzburg.o: Archbishop Hieronymus von Colloredo fled Salzburg before French troops in 1800. Under the Imperial Recess of 1803 the prince-archbishopric was secularised and given, together with Berchtesgaden and parts of Passau and Eichstätt, to Ferdinand III, the former Grand Duke of Tuscany, who received an electoral title.
electorate-of-salzburg.r: Ferdinand's brief rule brought a reorganised administration and a secular government in place of the archbishops, though the population remained Catholic. The university was continued, and Salzburg's economy still relied on salt mining at Hallein and trade. The electorate had little time to develop before war returned.
electorate-of-salzburg.e: After Austria's defeat at Austerlitz, the Peace of Pressburg in December 1805 gave Salzburg to the Austrian Empire, and Ferdinand was compensated with Würzburg. Salzburg later passed to Bavaria from 1810 to 1816 before returning permanently to Austria.

eblani.t: People of eastern Ireland named in Ptolemy's Geography, whose town Eblana has often, though doubtfully, been linked with Dublin.
eblani.o: The Eblani are known only from the Geography of Ptolemy, compiled around 150 from earlier sailors' reports. He places them on the east coast of Ireland, south of the Voluntii and north of the Cauci, roughly in the area of modern County Dublin and Meath, with a town called Eblana.
eblani.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, society or customs. The resemblance of Eblana to Dublin led older writers to identify the two, but most scholars now doubt the link, since Dublin's name is Irish and Ptolemy's coordinates are imprecise. Archaeology shows Roman goods reaching the east coast at sites such as Drumanagh.
eblani.e: The Eblani do not appear in any later source, and no Irish tradition preserves their name. Their area later fell within the territory of the Kingdom of Leinster and of the rising Uí Néill dynasties of Brega.

east-breifne.t: The O'Reilly lordship of County Cavan, a Gaelic state with its own coinage and a town at Cavan, until the Plantation of Ulster.
east-breifne.o: East Breifne emerged when the Kingdom of Breifne split in 1256 and the O'Reillys, Muintir Mhaoilmhordha, took the eastern part. They founded the town of Cavan around their castle at Clough Oughter and the Franciscan friary.
east-breifne.r: The O'Reillys traded with the Pale, and their 'O'Reilly money', clipped coins circulating in the 15th century, was common enough to be banned by the Irish Parliament in 1447. The lordship was organised in Gaelic fashion, with tanistry, brehon law and a hereditary learned class.
east-breifne.e: Under the Tudors the area became County Cavan in 1584. After the Nine Years' War and the Flight of the Earls it was included in the Plantation of Ulster from 1609, with lands granted to English and Scottish settlers.

emirate-of-bukhara.t: The Manghit state of Bukhara, a conservative Islamic emirate that survived as a Russian protectorate until the Red Army stormed its capital in 1920.
emirate-of-bukhara.o: Muhammad Rahim of the Manghit tribe took real power in the Khanate of Bukhara in the 1740s under Nader Shah's protection. In 1785 Shah Murad, a pious ruler, set aside the Janid figurehead khans and took the title emir, founding the Emirate of Bukhara.
emirate-of-bukhara.r: The emirs ruled through Uzbek tribal chiefs, a clerical elite and officials, enforcing Islamic law strictly. Bukhara had hundreds of mosques and madrasas and was a centre of trade in cotton, karakul and silk. Emir Nasrullah executed the British officers Stoddart and Conolly in 1842. Wars with the Khanate of Kokand and Khiva were frequent.
emirate-of-bukhara.e: Russia defeated Emir Muzaffar in 1868, taking Samarkand and making Bukhara a protectorate. In 1920 the Red Army and the Young Bukharans stormed Bukhara, the last emir, Alim Khan, fled to Afghanistan, and the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic was founded.

emirate-of-bitlis.t: A Kurdish emirate that ruled Bitlis for centuries and produced Sharaf Khan Bidlisi, author of the Sharafnama, the first history of the Kurds.
emirate-of-bitlis.o: Bitlis, at a gorge south-west of Lake Van, came under the Rojiki, a Kurdish tribal confederation, whose emirs claimed descent from ancient Kurdish lords. Their rule is traditionally dated from the late 12th century, though early details rest on the family's own later history.
emirate-of-bitlis.r: The emirs ruled from Bitlis castle over a mountain district controlling the road from Iran to the Tigris. After 1514 they accepted Ottoman suzerainty with hereditary autonomy, alternating between Ottoman and Safavid sides. Emir Sharaf Khan Bidlisi completed the Sharafnama in Persian in 1597, a history of Kurdish dynasties. Evliya Celebi described the rich court of Abdal Khan in 1655, shortly before an Ottoman army attacked him.
emirate-of-bitlis.e: In the 19th-century Ottoman centralisation the hereditary emirs were removed, and Bitlis was placed under appointed governors by 1849.

earldom-of-orkney.t: Norse earldom of the Orkney and Shetland islands, the heart of a sea-based power in northern Britain for six centuries, recorded in the Orkneyinga saga.
earldom-of-orkney.o: Norse settlers took over Orkney in the 9th century, displacing or absorbing the Pictish population. According to the Orkneyinga saga, Harald Fairhair granted the islands to Earl Rognvald of Møre, who passed them to his brother Sigurd, the first earl, in the late 9th century.
earldom-of-orkney.r: The earls owed allegiance to the kings of Norway, and later also to the kings of Scotland for Caithness, but often acted independently. Thorfinn the Mighty, in the 11th century, ruled much of northern Scotland and built a minster at Birsay. Earl Magnus, murdered around 1117, was venerated as a saint, and his nephew Rögnvald Kali Kolsson began St Magnus Cathedral in Kirkwall in 1137.
earldom-of-orkney.e: After the Norse line died out in 1231, Scottish families held the earldom, ending with the Sinclairs. In 1468 Christian I of Denmark-Norway pledged Orkney to James III of Scotland as security for his daughter Margaret's dowry, and in 1472 the earldom was annexed to the Scottish crown. Norse law and the Norn language lingered for centuries.
